extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of aesthetics and philosophy (those studying or applying Schopenhauer's theory of art)
extracted.subtask_short: aesthetic evaluation of beauty and sublime
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and explanatory principles for judging beauty, the sublime, and artistic worth according to Schopenhauer: when perception becomes 'pure knowing' (free from will), what counts as beautiful or sublime, and which artistic practices are admissible or reprehensible. Includes senses-ranking, examples, and implications for arts such as painting and architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light as condition of beauty and pure knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Light is the pleasantest and most gladdening of things; it is the correlative and condition of the most perfect kind of knowledge of perception, the only knowledge which does not in any way affect the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Light increases the beauty of objects (architectural beauty especially), produces transparent colours that excite delight, and explains the aesthetic delight in reflections in water. Pleasure from light is pleasure in the objective possibility of pure perceptive knowledge—delight in pure knowing and its method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking of the senses by relation to the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Sight (pure perception) has no immediate connection with the will; hearing, touch, smell and taste have progressively stronger links to the will, with smells and tastes being 'subjective' and most closely related to the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because sight affords the purest form of knowledge freed from will it is most æsthetic; sounds, touch, smells, tastes can be sensuously agreeable or painful and thus more ignoble for æsthetic contemplation. This ranking affects which sensory qualities are appropriate for art that aims at pure contemplation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic pleasure as delight in pure perceptive knowledge (subjective side)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic pleasure consists simply of delight in perceptive knowledge as such, in opposition to will—pleasure that arises from pure knowledge freed from all will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This subjective pleasure underlies appreciation of light, transparent colours, and reflected images; it explains why certain perceptual conditions (clarity, distinctness, transparent colour) heighten beauty by facilitating pure knowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the sublime (aesthetic condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sublime arises when objects that have a hostile relation to the human will are nevertheless contemplated by a beholder who forcibly detaches himself from his will and gives himself up entirely to knowledge, comprehending only the object's Idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key features: the object is threatening or unfavourable to will; the beholder consciously transcends will; contemplation is maintained despite recognition of hostility; result is spiritual exaltation. If a single real act of will (personal danger) enters consciousness, the impression of the sublime is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between beautiful and sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful: pure knowledge gains the upper hand without struggle because the object's properties facilitate recognition of its Idea. Sublime: pure knowledge is attained only by a conscious and forcible breaking away from the object's recognised hostile relation to the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus beauty involves ease of transition to pure, will-less knowing; sublimity involves effortful transcendence of the will and is accompanied by a remembrance of the will (not a particular volition, but human volition in general).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime accompanied by remembrance of will
rubrics_metrics.description: The exaltation of the sublime must be consciously won and consciously retained, so it is accompanied by a constant remembrance of will—not a single particular volition but human volition in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This remembrance distinguishes the sublime from the beautiful (where the will vanishes without a trace). If an immediate personal act of will (fear, desire, danger) arises, it destroys the contemplative peace and the sublime impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees and transitions of the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: There are varying degrees of the sublime and transitions from the beautiful to the sublime according as the additional quality (hostility of object to will) is strong, bold, urgent, near, or weak, distant, and merely indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: faint sublime in favourable winter light on cold stone; lonely motionless landscapes (prairies) as low sublime; deserts stripped of life as higher; storms, tempestuous seas and overwhelming natural forces as stronger degrees; highest degree occurs when both consciousness-as-individual and as pure knowing become sharply distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of sublime: dynamical and mathematical
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Kant’s nomenclature: dynamical sublime arises from the object's powerful hostility to the will (raging elements, cliffs, storms); mathematical sublime arises from presenting immensity in space or time, causing the individual to feel dwarfed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical sublime examples: high vast domes (St. Peter’s, St. Paul’s), starry heavens, contemplation of cosmic vastness or immense temporal duration (pyramids, ancient ruins). The experience ends in exultation when one recognises these worlds as appearances dependent on the subject of pure knowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime character (ethical dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sublime character is one in which the will is not excited by objects calculated to excite it; knowledge retains the upper hand in presence of provocations (e.g., injustice, others' happiness or beauty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a person observes faults without hatred, happiness without envy, perceives beauty without desire, and considers humanity more than personal lot—acting as knowing rather than suffering (example: Hamlet’s Horatio).

rubrics_metrics.name: The charming/attractive as opposite and forbidden in art
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper opposite of the sublime is 'the charming' or 'attractive,' which excites the will by presenting its fulfilment and so destroys pure aesthetic contemplation; it is unworthy of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two species: (1) Positive charming—e.g., Dutch still-lifes that deceptively excite appetite by representing food (painted fruit sometimes admissible but prepared dishes/beer/wine are condemned); naked figures in historical painting or sculpture designed to excite passion are condemned. (2) Negative charming—disgust or loathsomeness that arouses active aversion and the will; equally inadmissible in art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty defined as object of æsthetic contemplation (twofold meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: To call a thing beautiful means (a) it makes the spectator objective (pure will-less subject of knowing), and (b) we recognise in it not the particular thing but an Idea—the inner significance that is independent of relations and the principle of sufficient reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Everything can be observed objectively and therefore everything is potentially beautiful; degree of beauty depends on how easily the object facilitates pure contemplation or expresses a high grade of objectivity of will (human form and expression highest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of beauty depends on facilitation of pure contemplation
rubrics_metrics.description: One thing is more beautiful than another because it makes pure objective contemplation easier—it expresses the Idea of its species distinctly, or because the Idea it reveals is of a high grade of objectivity of will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human beings are more beautiful because they reveal rich, significant Ideas; inorganic and vegetable beauty tends to produce predominately the pleasure of pure will-less knowing, whereas animals and humans yield pleasure from comprehension of deeper Ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matter, manufactured articles, and what can express an Idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Matter as such cannot be the expression of an Idea; phenomena of an Idea must exhibit themselves in matter. Manufactured articles express the Idea of their material (forma substantialis) but not of their accidental form (forma accidentalis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rules out thinking that a table or chair expresses the Idea of 'table' or 'chair' in Plato’s sense; instead, the material qualities (gravity, rigidity, fluidity, light) are the Ideas revealed and thus can be objects of aesthetic contemplation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural aim: make low-grade Ideas distinct by prolonging conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture (considered purely as fine art apart from utility) aims to bring out distinctness of the lowest grades of objectivity of will—gravity, cohesion, rigidity, hardness—by making the conflict between such forces apparent and prolonged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architecture accomplishes this by depriving forces of the shortest way to satisfaction (e.g., roof presses to earth only through columns; arch supports itself via pillars), so that the struggle between gravity and rigidity becomes visible in many varied ways. If architecture serves useful ends (will), it ceases to be art in Schopenhauer's sense.
